prompt: What other proteins are related to histones, and describe that relationship using SCOPe classification levels.
answer:
In stable SCOPe release 2.08, the canonical nucleosome core histones H2A, H2B, H3, H4, and the histone domain of macro-H2A.1 belong to the same family, Nucleosome core histones (SUNID 47114; SCCS a.22.1.1). This is the closest relationship represented here.

Several other protein groups are more remotely related: they occupy different families within the shared Histone-fold superfamily (SUNID 47113; SCCS a.22.1), in the Histone-fold fold (SUNID 47112; a.22) and All alpha proteins class (SUNID 46456; a). These are the Archaeal histone family (SUNID 47129; a.22.1.2); the TBP-associated-factor family (SUNID 47134; a.22.1.3), which includes TAF(II)18, 28, 42, 62, the histone-fold domains of TAF4 and TAF12, CHRAC-14/16, NC2 alpha/beta, NF-YB/NF-YC, and the histone domain of Son of sevenless; and the Bacterial histone-fold-protein family (SUNID 101318; a.22.1.4), represented by Aq_328 and TTHA1479. SCOPe comments that the bacterial proteins contain two histone-fold repeats arranged like subunits of an archaeal histone dimer and that the 1wws structure forms dimers resembling the H3-H4 tetramer. Because these groups share a superfamily with core histones, SCOPe supports probable common ancestry of their classified domains, but their different families mark a weaker relationship than that among core histones. The a.22.1.0 automated-match bucket (SUNID 238448) is explicitly annotated “not a true family” and should not be interpreted as a coherent additional family.

Names can be misleading. The globular domains of linker histones H1/H5 are instead in the Linker histone H1/H5 family (SUNID 46827; a.4.5.13), within the Winged-helix DNA-binding superfamily (SUNID 46785; a.4.5). H-NS “histone-like” proteins likewise form a separate family (SUNID 81272; a.155.1.1), superfamily (SUNID 81273; a.155.1), and fold (SUNID 81274; a.155). Relative to core histones, these examples share only the broad all-alpha class; SCOPe therefore makes no superfamily-level homology assertion between them. That does not by itself prove convergence or absence of homology. Histone-modifying enzymes are also not homologous to histones merely because “histone” appears in their functional name.

These classifications apply to domains, not automatically to whole multidomain proteins. Superfamily membership does not justify transferring nucleosome assembly, DNA packaging, transcriptional function, interaction partners, oligomeric state, ligand specificity, or treating the proteins as interchangeable structural templates. Such stronger claims require domain-boundary-aware sequence alignments, structural superpositions and interface comparisons, compatible domain architecture, biochemical interaction/function evidence, and ideally phylogenetic or literature support. No best representative follows from this hierarchy; representative ranking would require quality records such as SPACI/AEROSPACI for every candidate.

prompt: What evolutionary relationship does SCOPe support between the MazG-like domain d1vmga_ and the HisE-like domain d1y6xa1, and what functional conclusions would go beyond that evidence?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, d1vmga_ (SUNID 113676; 1vmg chain A) is in the MazG-like family a.204.1.2 (SUNID 116993), whereas d1y6xa1 (SUNID 122676; 1y6x A:7–93) is in the HisE-like (PRA-PH) family a.204.1.4 (SUNID 140797). Their deepest shared homology-bearing node is the all-alpha NTP pyrophosphatases superfamily a.204.1 (SUNID 101386), within fold a.204 and the all-alpha class. Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry—a remote homologous relationship—but not family-level equivalence. The shared-superfamily annotation describes a five-helix active-site-forming module, but it does not establish identical chemistry. In particular, one must not transfer phosphoribosyl-ATP pyrophosphatase HisE activity, substrate specificity, catalytic residues, ligand preference, kinetics, oligomeric state, pathway role, or whole-protein function to d1vmga_; nor does the MazG-like label prove MazG-specific activity for d1y6xa1. The d1vmga_ comments that it is a structural-genomics target and is complexed with LI/UNL also do not establish substrate or physiological function. Such conclusions require external sequence and active-site comparisons, global structural alignment and ligand-bound structures, biochemical/kinetic assays, domain-context evidence, and ideally phylogenetic and literature support.

prompt: Actin/HSP70, hexokinase, and glycerol kinase have very different cellular roles. What relationship does SCOPe place among their catalytic domains, and what does that relationship permit you to infer?
answer: In stable SCOPe release 2.08, the classified catalytic domains belong to distinct families within the same Actin-like ATPase domain superfamily, c.55.1 (SUNID 53067): Actin/HSP70 is family c.55.1.1 (SUNID 53068), hexokinase is c.55.1.3 (SUNID 53083), and glycerol kinase is c.55.1.4 (SUNID 53089). Actin and HSP70 therefore have the closer, family-level placement, while all three groups share a superfamily-level relationship. This supports probable common ancestry of their classified domain cores—not merely a shared fold—despite their divergent cellular roles. The superfamily annotation also notes a duplication containing two domains of this fold, reinforcing that the inference applies to classified domains rather than automatically to entire multidomain proteins. This placement does not license transfer of actin polymerization, HSP70 chaperone activity, hexose or glycerol substrate specificity, detailed catalytic mechanism, regulation, oligomeric state, or pathway role, and it does not make the proteins interchangeable structural templates. Such stronger conclusions require domain-resolved sequence and structural alignments, conserved active-site residues in equivalent structural contexts, ligand-bound structures, biochemical substrate/kinetic evidence, domain-architecture analysis, and—where evolutionary history is claimed—phylogenetic or literature evidence.

prompt: How should the relationship among ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases be interpreted from SCOPe, given their different chemistries?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, these are three distinct families within one homology-bearing superfamily: Ferritin (SUNID 47241; a.25.1.1), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (SUNID 47253; a.25.1.2), and Manganese catalase/T-catalase (SUNID 100951; a.25.1.3). All descend from the Ferritin-like superfamily (SUNID 47240; a.25.1), within the Ferritin-like fold (SUNID 47239; a.25) and all-alpha class. Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry among their classified domains, not merely a shared fold. Their different chemistries are best interpreted as functional divergence among homologous families. The superfamily annotation notes a bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle, but neither this feature nor superfamily membership establishes identical metals, ligands, catalytic residues, redox intermediates, substrates, reactions, kinetics, regulation, oligomeric states, or whole-protein functions. In particular, ferritin iron-storage/mineralization behavior must not be transferred to RNR-like proteins or manganese catalases; RNR-like radical chemistry must not be transferred to the other families; and manganese-dependent peroxide disproportionation must not be inferred for ferritins or RNR-like proteins. A member of one family may be a remote template for the conserved structural core, but not automatically for active-site geometry, family-specific loops, domain architecture, oligomeric assembly, or functional annotation. A single representative also cannot stand for all three chemistries. Stronger mechanistic transfer requires family-aware sequence and active-site comparisons, global and ligand/metal-bound structural evidence, metal identification or spectroscopy, biochemical and kinetic assays, and ideally phylogenetic, domain-context, and literature support.

prompt: Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins, ephrin ectodomains, and the N-terminal domain of PAD4 appear biologically unrelated. What does SCOPe say about their relationship, and should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred across them?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, these are different families within the same homology-bearing Cupredoxins superfamily (b.6.1, SUNID 49503) and Cupredoxin-like fold (b.6, SUNID 49502): Plastocyanin/azurin-like is family b.6.1.1 (SUNID 49504; representative d1iuza_), Ephrin ectodomain is b.6.1.5 (SUNID 74874; d1ikop_), and the PAD4 N-terminal domain is b.6.1.6 (SUNID 110107; d5n0ya1, residues 3–112). Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry of these domains—not merely a similar fold—despite their different whole-protein biological roles. It does not make their families or functions equivalent.

Copper binding and electron transfer must not be transferred across them. Although the superfamily annotation mentions a copper-binding site and d1iuza_ is annotated as copper-complexed, SCOPe explicitly describes both the ephrin family and PAD4 N-terminal family as probably related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site. Superfamily membership alone therefore establishes neither copper coordination nor electron-transfer activity. Those claims require target-specific conservation of coordinating residues in a residue-level sequence/structure alignment, a metal-bound structure or spectroscopic coordination evidence, biochemical copper-binding measurements, and redox-potential or electron-transfer assays, with compatible domain and interaction context. Cross-family members may be fold templates after alignment and coverage inspection, but not interchangeable functional or active-site templates. The cited SIDs are classification examples, not quality-ranked universal representatives; d5n0ya1 also carries automated-match provenance, which does not itself validate function.

prompt: What biologically useful relationship does SCOPe support among ubiquitin-related proteins, UBX domains, and Ras-binding domains, and what annotation transfer would be unsafe?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the Ubiquitin-related family (SUNID 54237; SCCS d.15.1.1), UBX-domain family (SUNID 54250; d.15.1.2), and Ras-binding-domain/RBD family (SUNID 54263; d.15.1.5) are distinct families within the same Ubiquitin-like superfamily (SUNID 54236; d.15.1). Their deepest shared homology-bearing level is therefore the superfamily: SCOPe supports probable common ancestry and a conserved beta-grasp structural core (fold SUNID 54235; d.15), while the family split captures substantial sequence and functional divergence.

It would be unsafe to transfer family-specific annotations across that split—for example, to label UBX or RBD domains as ubiquitin-like modifiers or participants in ubiquitin conjugation, to infer UBX-associated VCP/p97 binding for ubiquitin-related or RBD domains, or to infer Ras/Rap-GTPase binding and effector specificity for ubiquitin-related or UBX domains. Nor does the shared superfamily make members interchangeable functional or interface templates, establish whole-protein function, or identify a best structural representative. Such transfers require family-resolved sequence and motif evidence, structural alignments and relevant complex/ligand-bound structures, conserved interface residues, compatible domain context, phylogenetic or literature support, and biochemical binding or conjugation assays; representative selection additionally requires quality records for every candidate.

prompt: CheY-related response regulators, an ornithine-decarboxylase N-terminal wing, and the KaiA N-terminal domain share a structural lineage in SCOPe. What relationship is supported, and which signaling or catalytic claims are not?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, these are three distinct families within the same CheY-like superfamily, c.23.1 (SUNID 52172), itself in the flavodoxin-like fold c.23: CheY-related, c.23.1.1 (SUNID 52173); ornithine-decarboxylase N-terminal “wing,” c.23.1.4 (SUNID 52252); and the KaiA N-terminal domain, c.23.1.5 (SUNID 82344). Sharing a superfamily supports remote homology/probable common ancestry of their classified domains, but their separation into families indicates substantial functional divergence.

This placement does not transfer CheY-family two-component signaling, phospho-Asp receiver chemistry, metal dependence, or switch behavior to the ornithine-decarboxylase wing or KaiA N-terminal domain; SCOPe specifically annotates the KaiA family as lacking canonical receiver-domain features. Conversely, it does not show that CheY-related or KaiA domains bind ornithine, PLP, or perform decarboxylation, nor even that the ODC wing itself contains the enzyme’s catalytic machinery. KaiA’s circadian-regulatory role likewise cannot be assigned to the other families. The domains may be structural templates for the conserved superfamily core only, not interchangeable active-site or functional templates, and the hierarchy supplies no basis for choosing a representative structure. Stronger claims require residue-level sequence and motif comparisons in equivalent structural positions, structural alignments, ligand/metal/cofactor-bound structures, whole-protein domain-context evidence, phylogeny or literature support, and direct phosphotransfer, binding, interaction, or catalytic assays.

prompt: Why is the bulge domain of the V1 ATP synthase A subunit classified separately from the other barrel-sandwich-hybrid superfamilies, and what evolutionary claim does that placement make?
answer: In SCOPe 2.08, the V1 ATP synthase A-subunit bulge domain (protein SUNID 310706) belongs to family b.84.5.1 (SUNID 310616) and its own superfamily, “V1 ATP synthase A subunit, bulge domain-like,” b.84.5 (SUNID 310577). It shares the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold b.84 (SUNID 51229)—described as a sandwich of half-barrel-shaped beta sheets—with four other superfamilies: single hybrid motif (b.84.1), rudiment single hybrid motif (b.84.2), duplicated hybrid motif (b.84.3), and ribosomal L27 protein-like (b.84.4). The separate placement means that SCOPe recognizes fold/topology-level structural similarity but does not consider the available evidence sufficient to assert superfamily-level common ancestry between b.84.5 and b.84.1–b.84.4. It positively supports probable common ancestry only among members placed within b.84.5. This is not a claim that the five superfamilies are proven nonhomologous, independently evolved, or convergent. Nor may ATP-synthase function, catalytic properties, motifs, ligand interactions, or interchangeable-template status be transferred to the other b.84 superfamilies from the shared fold. The API links b.84.5 to PubMed 19893485 but does not expose the curator’s detailed rationale; a stronger evolutionary explanation would require that literature plus global structural alignment, core-sequence correspondence, motifs compared in equivalent structural contexts, compatible domain context, and preferably phylogenetic or experimental evidence.

prompt: Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes, fumarate-reductase respiratory-complex transmembrane subunits, and respiratory nitrate-reductase gamma chains all use a heme-binding four-helical-bundle architecture. Does SCOPe support treating them as one homologous superfamily?
answer: No. In stable SCOPe 2.08, all three groups belong to the heme-binding four-helical-bundle fold f.21 (SUNID 81344), whose annotated core is an up-and-down bundle of four transmembrane helices binding one or two hemes. They are nevertheless assigned to three separate superfamilies: transmembrane di-heme cytochromes, f.21.1 (SUNID 81342); fumarate-reductase respiratory-complex transmembrane subunits, f.21.2 (SUNID 81343); and respiratory nitrate-reductase 1 gamma chain, f.21.3 (SUNID 103501). Thus SCOPe supports shared fold-level architecture, not one homologous superfamily. The fold’s homology record explicitly says that levels above superfamily do not imply homology. The f.21.3 annotation notes only a “possible link” and says this chain is structurally closer to FrdC; that comment is not a superfamily-level homology assertion or a merger of the three groups. Likewise, conserved heme ligands within f.21.1 and the single-chain-versus-two-chain organization within f.21.2 concern relationships inside those respective superfamilies, not across all three. Different SCOPe superfamilies also do not prove convergence, independent origin, or biological nonhomology. Those stronger conclusions would require external global structural alignments, core-sequence correspondence, ligand-coordinating motifs in equivalent structural contexts, compatible domain/complex context, phylogenetic analysis, and literature or experimental evidence. Shared f.21 membership alone does not justify transferring respiratory role, substrate/electron acceptor, heme stoichiometry or coordination geometry, chain organization, or treating representatives as interchangeable functional or homology templates; representative selection would additionally require quality evidence for every candidate.

prompt: How should a biologist interpret SCOPe's relationship among alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains, CoA-binding domains, and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains?
answer:
In stable SCOPe release 2.08, these are three distinct families: alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains (SUNID 51736; c.2.1.1), CoA-binding domains (SUNID 51900; c.2.1.8), and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains (SUNID 63944; c.2.1.9). Their deepest shared homology-bearing ancestor is the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily (SUNID 51735; c.2.1), within the correspondingly named fold (SUNID 51734; c.2) and alpha/beta class (SUNID 51349; c). Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry of the classified domains, while their separation into different families indicates substantial divergence; it does not place any pair in the closer same-family relationship.

The fold annotation describes a three-layer alpha/beta/alpha core with a six-stranded parallel beta sheet in order 321456. This shared architecture and superfamily placement must not be treated as proof of a shared present-day biochemical role. In particular, one must not transfer alcohol-dehydrogenase reaction chemistry or substrate specificity to the CoA-binding or potassium-channel families; infer CoA binding, NAD(P) specificity, catalytic activity, channel regulation, oligomeric state, or whole-protein function across the three; or assume that their structures are interchangeable modeling templates. The alcohol-dehydrogenase-like family also carries the comment that its N-terminal all-beta domain defines the family, making domain architecture important even though the classified entity named here is the C-terminal domain. The potassium-channel family’s automatic mapping to Pfam PF02254 is a cross-reference, not independent proof of identical function or of an automatically assigned SCOPe classification.

Stronger functional transfer or template choice would require domain-resolved sequence and structural alignments, conservation of catalytic or ligand-contacting residues in equivalent structural positions, ligand-bound structures, compatible domain architecture, and biochemical evidence—such as substrate/cofactor assays or channel-regulation measurements. Phylogenetic and literature evidence would be needed to refine the evolutionary history. Choosing a representative additionally requires boundaries and ASTRAL/SPACI or other quality data for every candidate; no best representative follows from family or superfamily membership alone. These conclusions apply to the classified domains, not automatically to their entire multidomain proteins.

prompt: In SCOPe 2.08, are d1s9za_ (Amyloidogenic design-1) and d1hqja_ (Unnamed design-1) homologous?
answer: No definitive homology claim is justified from this SCOPe grouping. In SCOPe 2.08, d1s9za_ (SUNID 98768; Amyloidogenic design-1, protein SUNID 103785) and d1hqja_ (SUNID 61142; Unnamed design-1, protein SUNID 100906) are nominally colocated in designed-protein class k, fold k.40, superfamily k.40.1 (SUNID 100904), and family k.40.1.1 (SUNID 100905). Although family and superfamily levels ordinarily carry a homology implication, this exact family has the curator annotation “not a true family”; its shared family code therefore must not be treated as positive pairwise homology evidence. The secure conclusion is shared designed trimeric coiled-coil classification, not demonstrated common ancestry. The caveat also does not prove that the designs are nonhomologous. Establishing a shared origin would require independent sequence correspondence plus documented design ancestry/template and literature evidence; structural similarity alone would establish topology, not genealogy. Amyloidogenicity must not be transferred from d1s9za_ to d1hqja_ without construct-specific aggregation or other biochemical/biophysical evidence.

prompt: Andreeva et al. 2008 describe PA1492 as a classification-change example. How did the relationship between PA1492 (PDB 1t1j) and nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase (PDB 1f8y) change between SCOP 1.69 and the current SCOPe release?
answer:
In SCOP 1.69, PA1492 and nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase were classified together only at class c, “Alpha and beta proteins (a/b)” (SUNID 51349). PA1492 chain A was d1t1ja_ (SUNID 106249), c.137.1.1: fold c.137, superfamily c.137.1, and family c.137.1.1, all named “Hypothetical protein PA1492.” By contrast, 1f8y chain A was d1f8ya_ (SUNID 31395), c.23.14.1: flavodoxin-like fold c.23 (SUNID 52171), N-deoxyribosyltransferase superfamily c.23.14 (SUNID 52309), and family c.23.14.1 (SUNID 52310). Thus 1.69 did not place them in the same fold or make a superfamily-level common-ancestry assertion; this does not prove that they were nonhomologous, analogous, or independently evolved. The B-chain copies had the corresponding same placements.

The current stable SCOPe release is 2.08. There, PA1492’s principal A-chain domain is d1t1ja1, A:1-118 (retaining SUNID 106249), reclassified as c.23.14.2. It now shares the flavodoxin-like fold c.23 and N-(deoxy)ribosyltransferase-like superfamily c.23.14 with d1f8ya_, while remaining in a separate PA1492 family c.23.14.2 (SUNID 110461) from the N-deoxyribosyltransferase family c.23.14.1. The B-chain domains show the same relationship (d1t1jb1 versus d1f8yb_). SCOPe 2.08 therefore supports probable common ancestry at the superfamily level, but not the closer relationship implied by a shared family. The 2.08 inventory also contains non-core l.1.1.1 records at A:0-0 and B:-6-0; they are not part of this PA1492-core comparison.

The annotations are consistent with, but do not by themselves prove the rationale for, the move: the old PA1492 fold was described as a four-stranded 2134 sheet, the flavodoxin-like fold as a five-stranded 21345 sheet, and the current PA1492 family as lacking the last strand, being monomeric, and having predicted deoxyribosyltransferase activity. The shared superfamily annotation notes similar active-site architectures and catalytic mechanisms among functionally characterized members. Nevertheless, the specific nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase activity, substrate/ligand specificity, and oligomeric behavior of 1f8y cannot be transferred to PA1492; “predicted” activity is not biochemical confirmation. Nor is 1f8y automatically an interchangeable structural or functional template, especially given PA1492’s missing strand and monomer annotation. Stronger claims require the Andreeva et al. paper or curator rationale, a residue-resolved structural and sequence alignment with active-site correspondence and coverage, ligand-bound evidence for PA1492, biochemical substrate/activity assays, and compatible oligomeric/domain context. The retrieved API records verify the before-and-after classification, not the paper’s detailed evidentiary argument for why it changed.

prompt: SCOPe 2.08 divides PDB 1a14 chain H into d1a14h1 covering residues 9-111 and d1a14h2 covering residues 1-8. What is the second segment, and should similarity to it be treated as protein homology evidence?
answer: In SCOPe 2.08, d1a14h2 (SUNID 343393; residues H:1–8; SCCS l.1.1.1) is a synthetic N-terminal tag, classified under class l “Artifacts” and the Tags hierarchy—not a second natural protein domain. By contrast, d1a14h1 (H:9–111; SCCS b.1.1.1) is the immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable domain. The d1a14h2 homology record explicitly says that class-l artifacts are not homology evidence, so sequence or structural similarity to this eight-residue tag must not support protein ancestry, function transfer, or template selection. Establishing homology would instead require evidence from genuine non-tag regions, such as substantial sequence and structural correspondence in biological domains, supported where appropriate by domain-context and phylogenetic evidence.

prompt: How did the SCOP 1.75 domain definitions for PDB 1acc chain A change in newer releases of SCOPe? What does the change reveal about domains as evolutionary modules, and how should it affect homology searches?
answer:
In SCOP 1.75, chain A of PDB 1acc was one domain, d1acca_ (SUNID 43828), covering “A:” and classified as family f.11.1.1 in the Anthrax protective antigen superfamily/fold. Stable SCOPe 2.07 and 2.08 instead contain two domains: the N-terminal d1acca2 (SUNID 238522; A:14-225), family b.179.1.1 “PA14,” superfamily b.179.1 “PA14-like,” fold b.179, all-beta class b; and the C-terminal d1acca1 (SUNID 238521; A:226-735), family f.60.1.1, superfamily f.60.1, and fold f.60 “Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like,” in class f. Thus the former whole-chain domain was replaced by two adjacent, separately classified regions; residues outside the reported ranges are not assigned to either retrieved domain.

Biologically, this illustrates that a PDB chain is not necessarily one evolutionary unit. Separately classifiable domains can be combined in one protein and recognized in other evolutionary contexts. SCOPe supports family/superfamily homology searches separately for the PA14-like N-terminal module and the C-terminal-like module. Because these two modules have different classes, folds, and superfamilies, SCOPe makes no homology assertion between them—but that alone does not prove convergence or independent origin.

Homology searches should therefore use residues 14-225 and 226-735 as separate queries or apply domain-aware methods. A hit to one region supports a relationship only for that module: it must not be extended automatically to the other domain or to the complete protective-antigen chain. Likewise, toxin/protective-antigen function, calcium binding, receptor specificity, reaction or ligand specificity, oligomeric behavior, and whole-protein architecture cannot be transferred from a domain-level match alone. A structure matched to one module is not automatically an interchangeable full-chain template. Such conclusions require residue-resolved sequence and structural alignments, coverage and topology assessment, conserved functional residues in equivalent contexts, ligand-bound or biochemical evidence, compatible domain architecture, and where relevant phylogenetic or literature support. The retrieved API records establish that the split occurred but do not expose the curator’s alignment or literature rationale. No structural-quality comparison was retrieved, so they also do not select a best representative.

prompt: What does SCOPe's five-domain decomposition of Prp8 in PDB 3jb9 reveal about its evolutionary history? Which domains are related to previously characterized proteins, and which represents a newly observed fold?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, Prp8 is chain A of 3jb9 and is decomposed into five domains, revealing an evolutionary mosaic rather than one uniformly derived globular domain. From N to C terminus: d3jb9a5 (A:47–697; d.394.1.1) is the distinctive N-terminal Prp8/Spp42 domain; SCOPe assigns it the newly observed Prp8 N-terminal fold d.394 (SUNID 345891), whose annotated core is mainly helical with several small beta sheets. d3jb9a4 (A:698–822; a.29.2.1) belongs to the bromodomain family. d3jb9a3 (A:823–1604; e.8.1.8) is the Prp8 reverse-transcriptase domain within the DNA/RNA-polymerase superfamily e.8.1. d3jb9a2 (A:1605–1780; c.52.1.36) is a Prp8 endonuclease-like domain within the restriction-endonuclease-like superfamily c.52.1. d3jb9a1 (A:1784–2030; c.55.3.14) is the Prp8 beta-finger domain within the RNase-H-like superfamily c.55.3. Thus the bromodomain, polymerase/RT, restriction-endonuclease-like, and RNase-H-like modules have relationships to previously characterized protein groups at family or superfamily strength, whereas the large N-terminal region represents the Prp8-specific new fold. Superfamily membership supports probable common ancestry, but it does not establish that Prp8 retains the corresponding polymerase, nuclease, RNase-H, ligand-binding, or bromodomain biochemical activities. Nor does SCOPe determine the order or mechanism by which these modules were assembled. Those stronger conclusions require sequence alignments, structural superpositions, active-site and ligand-bound structural evidence, biochemical assays, domain-context analysis, phylogenetics, and relevant literature.

prompt: Why do d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_ all belong to TAL effector family a.298.1.1 in SCOPe despite vastly different sequence lengths?
answer:
In SCOPe 2.08, d2kq5a_ (PthA), d3v6pa_ (dHax3), and d4cj9a_ (BurrH) all have the same lineage: all-alpha class a, left-handed alpha-alpha-superhelix fold a.298, TAL-effector-like superfamily a.298.1, and TAL-effector family a.298.1.1 (family SUNID 267609). The shared family—the deepest relevant homology-bearing level—supports a close relationship despite their different total lengths.

The explanation is repeat-number variation. SCOPe marks this as an `re` case: the common domain is composed of different numbers of small repeating units. Its family record identifies 4cj9 A:259-292 as the canonical representative repeat; those coordinates apply to d4cj9a_, not to the other domains. The original SEQRES domain sequences are 51 residues for d2kq5a_, 373 for d3v6pa_, and 752 for d4cj9a_. d2kq5a_ is explicitly annotated “single repeat,” whereas the longer sequences contain extended repeat arrays. Thus, SCOPe groups them by the homologous repeat module and shared repeat architecture, not by requiring equal array length.

This placement does not establish identical repeat counts, DNA-binding specificity, biochemical activity, whole-protein function, or interchangeable full-length templates. In particular, the 51-residue single-repeat structure may represent a local repeat core but cannot automatically model the complete 373- or 752-residue arrays. Stronger transfer would require unit-by-unit sequence alignment, structural superposition of corresponding repeats, matched domain/terminal context, target-bound structural evidence, biochemical specificity measurements, and—where evolutionary history is claimed—phylogenetic or literature evidence.

prompt: What stable release and latest periodic update are reported by the current-release endpoint? Which identifier should be cited for a reproducible analysis, and what does the periodic label mean?
answer: The current-release endpoint reports stable release 2.08 (stable label `2.08-stable`; freeze date 2021-07-28, release date 2021-09-22) and latest periodic update `2.08-2026-08-16`, dated 2026-08-16. For reproducible analysis, cite and query the stable release selector `2.08` (optionally noting its `2.08-stable` label), not the dated periodic label. The periodic label identifies the latest dated update associated with the 2.08 series; it does not replace the stable release or, by itself, establish which records were added or whether any particular classification changed. Verifying such changes requires comparing the relevant records across releases or obtaining a returned history record.

prompt: Early structures 1br0 and 1ez3 contained fragments of the syntaxin N-terminal domain, whereas 1dn1 chain B showed the full domain. How should SCOPe's current treatment of these structures change the biological interpretation of fragment-based fold assignments?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, 1br0 domain d1br0a_ (SUNID 17772), all three 1ez3 domains d1ez3a_/b_/c_ (SUNIDs 17768–17770), and 1dn1 chain-B domain d1dn1b_ (SUNID 302344) are all placed in all-alpha class a, STAT-like fold a.47, t-SNARE superfamily a.47.2, and t-SNARE family a.47.2.1. Thus their strongest current relationship is shared family—not merely shared fold—and the early structures should be interpreted as partial observations of the syntaxin-1A N-terminal/t-SNARE domain.

SCOPe preserves the limitation explicitly: d1br0a_ and every 1ez3 domain are described as a “three-helical fragment; similar to one spectrin repeat” and carry the `ms` inconsistency for missing secondary structures comprising less than one-third of the common domain. The STAT-like fold itself is described as a four-long-helix bundle. Consequently, the fragments’ local spectrin-repeat resemblance must not be promoted to a complete-domain fold model or to evidence of spectrin ancestry. Fold-level resemblance alone would not imply homology; here the positive relationship to the complete syntaxin domain instead comes from their common t-SNARE superfamily and family. Missing fragment positions must not be interpreted as biological deletions.

The fragments are also unsafe as interchangeable templates for an intact domain: they cannot establish packing of the missing helix, full-domain conformational state, interaction geometry, oligomeric state, or detailed membrane-fusion mechanism. Those transfers require a complete-domain structural alignment with residue mapping, full-domain sequence evidence, and appropriate biochemical, interaction, conformational, or literature evidence. Representative selection additionally needs comparable quality records for every candidate. SCOPe records 1dn1 as obsolete and replaced by 3c98, and labels d1dn1b_ an automated match to d3c98b_; automation is provenance, not evidence of poor quality, and the retrieved records do not justify a quality ranking. Finally, the API establishes the present classification and fragment caveats, but not the historical curator reasoning; a claim about when or why an earlier assignment changed would require release-by-release records plus the relevant alignment or literature.

prompt: NAD(P)-binding enzymes occur in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies. What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, NAD(P)-associated domains occupy genuinely different structural groups: the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann superfamily c.2.1 (SUNID 51735) lies in fold c.2; the DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding superfamily c.31.1 (SUNID 52467) lies in fold c.31; and the HMG-CoA-reductase NAD-binding family d.58.20.1 (SUNID 55036) lies in superfamily d.58.20 and the ferredoxin-like fold d.58, even in a different SCOPe class. SCOPe also notes that c.31.1 binds its cofactor in the opposite direction from the classical Rossmann fold, while c.2 has nucleotide-binding modes similar to nearby folds.

The evolutionary implication is level-dependent. Members of one family have the closest SCOPe relationship; membership in one superfamily supports probable common ancestry followed by divergence, although it does not establish identical chemistry. Across different superfamilies—and especially different folds—the recurrence of NAD(P) binding is consistent with convergent recruitment of the same chemically useful cofactor by distinct structural solutions. It is not, however, proof that every such pair evolved independently: the retrieved fold records explicitly say that homology is not implied above the superfamily level, which is an absence of a positive SCOPe homology assertion rather than proof of nonhomology.

Cofactor binding or local active-site resemblance alone is insufficient because selection by the same ligand and reaction chemistry can favor similar local geometries or short motifs without shared ancestry; local resemblance does not establish correspondence across the whole domain core. Conversely, divergent homologs can retain ancestry while changing substrate, NAD versus NADP preference, catalytic residues, mechanism, or overall function. Therefore one must not transfer exact reaction, substrate specificity, cofactor preference, stereochemistry, catalytic mechanism, whole-protein function, or assume interchangeable structural templates from NAD(P) binding or active-site similarity alone. Stronger convergence or remote-homology claims require external global structural alignments and topology, statistically supported sequence correspondence across equivalent core positions, motifs compared in equivalent structural contexts, verified domain boundaries and architectures, phylogenetic evidence, and ligand-bound biochemical or mutational evidence. Template selection should remain within a verified homologous family or superfamily where possible and still be checked for domain context, active-site conservation, ligand state, and biochemical specificity.

prompt: How did the relationship between the ColG collagenase domain in PDB 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in PDB 1dlc change from SCOPe 2.04 to current SCOPe, and what structural and functional evidence supports their common ancestry?
answer:
SCOPe 2.04 did not classify the ColG and Cry3A domains as homologs: ColG copies d1nqda_ and d1nqdb_ were in the CUB-like fold, collagen-binding superfamily and family b.23.2.1, whereas Cry3A C-terminal domain d1dlca1 (A:500–644) was in the galactose-binding-domain-like fold/superfamily and delta-endotoxin C-terminal family b.18.1.3. They shared only the all-beta class, which is not homology-bearing; this old separation was not proof of independent origin.

The current public stable release is SCOPe 2.08. It moves the biological ColG domain into the galactose-binding-domain-like fold and superfamily b.18.1, as the distinct collagen-binding family b.18.1.36 (SUNID 267607). Cry3A remains family b.18.1.3 (SUNID 49796). Thus the deepest shared level is now superfamily b.18.1 (SUNID 49785): SCOPe supports probable common ancestry, but not a same-family relationship. For chain B, the biological ColG region is now d1nqdb1, residues 893–1008; residues 891–892 are separately classified as synthetic tag d1nqdb2 and must not be used as homology evidence. Chain-A copy d1nqda_ retains its SID while changing from b.23.2.1 to b.18.1.36.

Structural support is remote rather than sequence-obvious. SCOPe annotates the ColG family with PMID 17977833 as describing likely homology among ColG d1nqdb_, the Cry4Ba C-terminal domain d1w99a3, and CPE C-terminal domain d2quoa_. Cry4Ba d1w99a3 and Cry3A d1dlca1 are in the same delta-endotoxin C-terminal family b.18.1.3, so Cry4Ba supplies a close family bridge to Cry3A. In the stored FATCAT evidence, 1nqdA maps to representative chain 1nqjA at 99.16% sequence identity over 119 alignment columns; that representative has a structural match to d1w99a3 with P=0.00395, RMSD 2.52 Å, and only 2.5% reported identity, consistent with a deeply diverged shared beta-sandwich core. This is representative-mediated evidence, not a direct 1nqd–1dlc superposition.

The functional context is compatible with diversification of an ancestral target-binding module: ColG uses this domain for collagen binding, Cry C-terminal domains contribute host/receptor or carbohydrate recognition and specificity, and the cited bridge d2quoa_ is a beta-sandwich claudin-4-binding domain. That broad binding-role coherence supports the structural relationship but cannot establish homology by itself. Collagen specificity, Cry3A receptor specificity, insecticidal activity, calcium dependence, catalytic chemistry, and whole-protein function must not be transferred between the families. Likewise, b.18.1 membership supports using one structure only as a core-fold/topology template, not as an interchangeable binding-site, loop, ligand-bound-state, or multidomain-architecture template. A stronger mechanistic account requires the direct 1nqd–1dlc structural alignment, core sequence correspondence, ligand/receptor-bound structures, biochemical binding data, phylogeny, and inspection of PMID 17977833; the retrieved API exposes the citation and classification but not that paper’s detailed argument.

prompt: d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 share homeodomain family a.4.1.1, but d1ztra1 has an hf annotation. What remains justified about homology, and why should the structures not be treated as interchangeable templates or training examples?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, d1p7jd_ (SUNID 94286) and d1ztra1 (SUNID 125655) share the Homeodomain family a.4.1.1 (SUNID 46690), Homeodomain-like superfamily a.4.1 (46689), and even the Engrailed Homeodomain protein and Drosophila melanogaster species nodes. Their shared family therefore continues to support a close homologous relationship and probable common ancestry; the hf annotation does not erase that relationship.

The qualification is structural. d1ztra1 has a domain-level, non-inherited hf annotation stating that it adopts a different fold from the exemplar despite similar sequence and number of secondary structures. Consequently, family membership must not be converted into an assumption that d1ztra1 and d1p7jd_ have interchangeable topology, coordinates, residue correspondences, binding geometry, or conformational state. The API does not establish that d1p7jd_ itself is the exemplar, so the annotation also does not by itself prove a specific pairwise structural difference; that requires direct structural comparison. Both entries are annotated as mutants, and d1p7jd_ is additionally described as complexed with NHE, further limiting unqualified transfer of native structure, interactions, DNA-recognition specificity, or biochemical function.

For modeling, interchangeability would require a direct structure alignment with topology and coverage assessment, sequence alignment including the mutations, experimental-state and complex/partner evidence, and structure-quality measurements for both candidates. For datasets, they may be retained as homologous examples only with the hf caveat preserved. They should be excluded or separately stratified when the label assumes one uniform fold, and they should not be placed across independent train/test splits without sequence-clustering or ASTRAL-style nonredundancy controls: their shared protein/species lineage and the hf combination of similar sequence with altered fold create both leakage and label-confounding risks.

prompt: d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 belong to fibronectin type III family b.1.2.1, but d1o5dt2 is annotated as a fragment. How should that annotation affect alignment, representative selection, and interpretation of family diversity?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, d1uc6a1 (SUNID 107766; 1uc6 A:6–109) and d1o5dt2 (SUNID 103884; 1o5d T:107–205) share the Fibronectin type III superfamily b.1.2 (SUNID 49265) and family b.1.2.1 (SUNID 49266), supporting a close family-level relationship. That relationship is not erased by the fragment annotation. However, d1o5dt2 has a domain-scoped `fr` caveat: “fragment; missing more than one-third of the common structure and/or sequence.”

Alignment should therefore be boundary- and coverage-aware: align only the observed homologous core, report coverage, and treat positions absent from d1o5dt2 as missing data—not as biological deletions, family-specific indels, or evidence of structural divergence. Full-length sequence and structure alignments are needed before interpreting those regions evolutionarily.

For representative selection, d1o5dt2 should not be the sole representative of a complete FnIII domain or a full-domain modeling template. Its PDB entry has higher entry-level SPACI/AEROSPACI than 1uc6 (0.28747 versus 0.02158) and is a 2.05 Å X-ray structure, whereas 1uc6 is NMR with no crystallographic resolution; nevertheless, technical quality cannot compensate for missing domain content. Retain d1o5dt2 when the covered core or its complexed state is relevant, but label or stratify it as a fragment and select a completeness-verified domain for full-domain representation. No `fr` caveat was returned for d1uc6a1, but absence of a machine-readable warning alone does not prove completeness.

The missing portion must not be counted as natural family diversity. Estimate family diversity from multiple complete, nonredundant representatives using coverage-aware sequence and structural alignments, while analyzing fragments separately. Family membership also does not justify transferring tissue-factor function, ciliary-neurotrophic-factor-receptor function, ligand specificity, binding partners, or template interchangeability between these domains. Such transfer requires complete-domain sequence/structure evidence, compatible domain context, ligand-bound structures, biochemical data, and—where evolutionary breadth is claimed—phylogenetic or literature support.

prompt: A newly solved domain resembles a known SCOPe fold but lacks convincing evidence of common ancestry with any existing superfamily. Should it be assigned to a new family, a new superfamily in the existing fold, or a new fold? What biological claim does each choice make?
answer: Assign it to a new superfamily within the existing fold, assuming the fold-level topological resemblance is convincing. This records structural similarity while making no positive SCOPe assertion of common ancestry with existing superfamilies. A new family under an existing superfamily would make the stronger evolutionary claim that the domain probably shares a common origin with that superfamily, while distinguishing a closer subgroup; the stated evidence does not support that. A new fold would claim that its major secondary-structure arrangement and topology differ sufficiently from existing folds, so lack of homology evidence alone is not grounds for that choice. These placements are hypotheses that may change with stronger evidence: global structural alignment, core sequence correspondence, motifs in equivalent structural contexts, compatible domain architecture and biological context, phylogenetic support, experiments, or relevant literature. Fold membership alone cannot justify transferring function, substrate, mechanism, ligand specificity, active-site residues, or treating an existing domain as an interchangeable modeling template. Template choice additionally requires alignment coverage, residue mapping, conformational and domain-context compatibility, and structure-quality evidence for every candidate; SPACI/AEROSPACI would assess representative quality, not homology. The consulted API identifies SCOPe 2.08 as the current stable release, but no entity-specific identifier applies to this hypothetical domain.

prompt: Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the three catalytic-domain groups are distinct families within the same Protein kinase-like superfamily d.144.1 (SUNID 56112) and fold d.144: canonical protein-kinase catalytic subunits are d.144.1.7 (SUNID 88854), aminoglycoside/APH phosphotransferases are d.144.1.6 (SUNID 64411), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic domains are d.144.1.4 (SUNID 56171). Their shared superfamily supports probable common ancestry of the classified catalytic cores—stronger than mere fold similarity—and a shared kinase-like structural framework compatible with nucleotide-dependent phosphoryl transfer. It does not make them members of one close family, establish identical catalytic details, or extend homology to every region of the full-length proteins.

Substrate specificity and regulation are unsafe to transfer across these families. In particular, protein/peptide recognition and activation-loop-style control from canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside-antibiotic specificity from APHs, and phosphoinositide head-group recognition, membrane targeting, and class-specific partner regulation from PI3Ks cannot be inferred from d.144.1 membership. Nor does the classification establish shared inhibitor sensitivity, nucleotide preference, regulatory partners, localization, oligomeric state, or pathway role.

A stronger transfer requires target-specific evidence: sequence alignment showing conservation of catalytic and specificity residues in equivalent structural positions; structural superposition and preferably substrate-, nucleotide-, and cofactor-bound structures defining the relevant pockets; biochemical kinetics and binding assays with the proposed donor and acceptor substrates; mutational tests of catalytic and recognition residues; and, for regulation, full-length domain-context, conformational, post-translational-modification, membrane-association, interaction-partner, cellular, and phylogenetic evidence. SCOPe hierarchy alone supplies none of those substrate- or regulation-specific demonstrations.
